questions.question: Can people cooperate even if they don't fully agree on everything? / (Yes/No) Explain briefly.
questions.solution_html:
• Yes, people can cooperate even without complete agreement because cooperation is often
  • based on common interests or shared goals. In society, individuals and groups may differ in
  • opinions, beliefs, or values but still work together for mutual benefit.
  • For example, political parties may cooperate in a coalition government despite ideological
  • differences. Similarly, workers in an organization cooperate to complete tasks even if they
  • disagree personally.
  • Sociologists view cooperation as an essential social process that promotes social order
  • integration, and collective survival. Mutual tolerance, compromise, and communication help
  • maintain cooperation.
questions.final_answer: maintain cooperation

questions.question: How do structural factors impact social mobility?
questions.solution_html:
• Structural factors significantly influence opportunities for social mobility. These include
  • education, economic conditions, caste, class, gender, and government policies.
  • People born into wealthy families often have better access to quality education and
  • employment opportunities, while disadvantaged groups face barriers. In India, caste
  • inequalities continue to affect occupational mobility and social status.
  • Gender discrimination may limit women’s mobility, whereas affirmative action and welfare
  • schemes can enhance opportunities for marginalized groups. Thus, social mobility is shaped
  • not only by individual effort but also by social structures.
questions.final_answer: not only by individual effort but also by social structures

questions.question: Critically assess the role of the media in reinforcing gender roles.
questions.solution_html:
• Critically Assess the Role of Media in Reinforcing Gender Roles
  • Media plays a major role in shaping ideas about masculinity and femininity. Television, films
  • advertisements, and social media often portray stereotypical gender roles.
  • Women are frequently represented as emotional, dependent, or concerned with beauty
  • while men are portrayed as strong and dominant. Such portrayals reinforce patriarchal
  • attitudes and unequal gender expectations.
  • Advertisements often associate women with household work and men with leadership
  • positions. This influences children’s perceptions from an early age.
  • However, media can also challenge stereotypes by promoting women’s empowerment
  • gender equality, and diverse identities. Therefore, media has both reinforcing and
  • transformative roles in relation to gender.
questions.final_answer: transformative roles in relation to gender

questions.question: Explain how peer groups impact adolescent socialization
questions.solution_html:
• Peer groups are important agents of socialization during adolescence. Adolescents spend
  • considerable time with friends and companions of similar age.
  • Peer groups influence behaviour, language, dressing style, attitudes, and interests. They help
  • adolescents develop self-identity, independence, confidence, and social skills.
  • Positive peer influence can encourage academic achievement and healthy behaviour, while
  • negative peer pressure may lead to deviance, substance abuse, or risky behaviour.
  • Thus, peer groups play a significant role in personality development and social adjustment.
questions.final_answer: Thus, peer groups play a significant role in personality development and social adjustment

questions.question: Explain how differential association theory interprets deviance.
questions.solution_html:
• Differential Association Theory was developed by Edwin H. Sutherland. According to the
  • theory, deviant behaviour is learned through interaction with others.
  • Individuals learn techniques, motives, values, and attitudes favourable to deviance from
  • intimate groups such as friends or peer groups. When people are exposed more to
  • definitions supporting deviance than opposing it, they are more likely to engage in deviant
  • acts.
  • For example, a teenager may learn criminal behaviour from delinquent peers. Therefore
  • deviance is not inherited but socially learned.
questions.final_answer: deviance is not inherited but socially learned

questions.question: Elucidate the role of intersectionality in understanding gender inequality / ?
questions.solution_html:
• Elucidate the Role of Intersectionality in Understanding Gender Inequality
  • Intersectionality is a concept developed mainly by Kimberlé Crenshaw to explain how
  • different forms of inequality interact and overlap. Gender inequality cannot be understood
  • in isolation because women experience discrimination differently based on caste, class, race
  • religion, ethnicity, sexuality, and disability.
  • For example, upper-class women and poor women face different social realities. Similarly
  • Dalit women in India experience both caste discrimination and gender oppression
  • simultaneously. Thus, intersectionality highlights multiple and interconnected forms of
  • disadvantage.
  • Key Features of Intersectionality
questions.final_answer: Key Features of Intersectionality

questions.question: Discuss the various strategies individuals and social groups employ to manage role strain and role conflict.
questions.solution_html:
• Strain and Role Conflict
  • Role strain occurs when a person faces difficulties in fulfilling multiple expectations
  • associated with a single role. Role conflict occurs when expectations from different roles
  • clash with each other.
  • For example, a working mother may experience conflict between professional duties and
  • family responsibilities.
  • Strategies to Manage Role Strain and Role Conflict
questions.final_answer: Strategies to Manage Role Strain and Role Conflict
